title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
setting: Baker Street, then Dartmoor in October: Baskerville Hall and its yew alley, Merripit House, the Grimpen Mire and the prehistoric huts on the moor
lengthNote: Fifteen chapters, about 60,000 words; chapters VIII to X are Watson’s letters to Holmes and extracts from his diary
openingLine: Mr. Sherlock Holmes ... was seated at the breakfast table.
summary: Dr James Mortimer brings Sherlock Holmes an eighteenth-century manuscript about a spectral hound that has haunted the Baskervilles since the wicked Hugo, and the story of Sir Charles Baskerville, found dead in his yew alley with, some distance off, the footprints of a gigantic hound. The heir, Sir Henry, arrives from Canada, receives a warning made of words cut from The Times, and loses two boots in his hotel. Holmes sends Watson to Dartmoor with him, where Watson meets the naturalist Stapleton and his beautiful sister, follows a butler signalling on to the moor, and sees a stranger standing on a tor. The stranger is Holmes. Together they expose Stapleton, a Baskerville under a false name with a real hound painted with phosphorus, who vanishes into the Grimpen Mire.
referenceStyle: chapter, numbered I to XV as the 1902 edition numbers them

sourceText.label: The Hound of the Baskervilles (London: George Newnes, 1902), two Internet Archive scans of the first edition
sourceText.note: The first London edition of 25 March 1902, which this edition prints. Its readings differ in places from the Project Gutenberg texts, which follow other printings: in 1902 Sir Charles dies on the 4th of June (Gutenberg has May), Watson cries Good heavens where they have My God, and the spelling is British throughout. Quotations follow the 1902 edition.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In nine monthly parts in The Strand Magazine, August 1901 to April 1902, with sixty illustrations by Sidney Paget.

atAGlance.label: In book form
atAGlance.note: Published by George Newnes in London on 25 March 1902, with sixteen of Paget’s illustrations; McClure, Phillips followed in New York in April.

atAGlance.label: The narrator
atAGlance.note: Watson tells the story, and in the middle of the book hands it over to his letters to Holmes and the diary he kept on the moor.

atAGlance.label: The source
atAGlance.note: Conan Doyle credited his friend Bertram Fletcher Robinson with the West-Country legend behind the story and with help on its plot and local details.

structure.label: Chapters I–V
structure.title: Baker Street
structure.summary: Holmes and Watson read a stick left by a visitor, who turns out to be Dr Mortimer of Grimpen. He reads them the legend of Hugo Baskerville and the hound, and tells them how Sir Charles died in the yew alley, running, with the footprints of a gigantic hound nearby. Sir Henry arrives from Canada to a warning pasted from The Times and a missing boot. A bearded man shadows him from a cab and escapes, and the cabman reports that his fare gave his name as Sherlock Holmes.

scenes.title: Mr. Sherlock Holmes
scenes.summary: A Penang lawyer, a curly-haired spaniel, and a doctor who covets Holmes’s skull.

scenes.title: The Curse of the Baskervilles; The Problem
scenes.summary: The manuscript of 1742, the Devon County Chronicle, the footprints, and a map of the moor studied all day in a cloud of shag.

scenes.title: Sir Henry Baskerville; Three Broken Threads
scenes.summary: Words cut from a Times leader, two stolen boots, a spy in a hansom, and a cabman with a message.

structure.label: Chapters VI–VII
structure.title: Baskerville Hall
structure.summary: Watson travels to Devon with Sir Henry and Mortimer. Soldiers watch the roads for Selden, an escaped murderer. At the gloomy Hall the black-bearded butler Barrymore lies about a woman sobbing in the night. On the moor Watson meets the naturalist Stapleton, who shows him the Grimpen Mire swallowing a pony, and hears a long moan across the moor. Stapleton’s sister, mistaking Watson for Sir Henry, urges him to go straight back to London.

scenes.title: Baskerville Hall
scenes.summary: A mounted soldier on the skyline, twin towers, a dining-hall of ancestors, and a sob in the night.

scenes.title: The Stapletons of Merripit House
scenes.summary: The great Grimpen Mire, a moth called Cyclopides, and a warning on a moorland path.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–IX
structure.title: Watson’s reports
structure.summary: Watson’s letters to Holmes describe the moor and its prehistoric huts, old Frankland and his telescope, and Sir Henry’s growing love for Miss Stapleton, which her brother furiously interrupts before apologising. Watson and Sir Henry catch Barrymore signalling from a window: the convict Selden is Mrs Barrymore’s younger brother, and they feed him on the moor. Hunting Selden, the two men hear the hound’s cry, and Watson sees a tall figure standing on a tor against the moon.

scenes.title: First Report of Dr. Watson
scenes.summary: Stone huts, a litigious neighbour, and a candle carried down a corridor at two in the morning.

scenes.title: Second Report of Dr. Watson
scenes.summary: An interrupted proposal, a light answered on the moor, a convict’s face over a rock, and a man on the tor.

structure.label: Chapters X–XI
structure.title: The man on the tor
structure.summary: Barrymore reveals that Sir Charles went to the gate to meet a woman with the initials L. L., and that another man is hiding on the moor. Watson finds Laura Lyons in Coombe Tracey; she admits writing to Sir Charles but says she never kept the appointment. From Frankland’s roof Watson spots a boy carrying food, follows him to a stone hut, finds a note reporting his own movements, and waits in the dark for the tenant. It is Holmes.

scenes.title: Extract from the Diary of Dr. Watson
scenes.summary: L. L., a burnt letter, a lost spaniel, and another man upon the moor.

scenes.title: The Man on the Tor
scenes.summary: Mrs Lyons at her typewriter, Frankland’s telescope, and a well-known voice at the door of the hut.

structure.label: Chapters XII–XIII
structure.title: Death on the moor
structure.summary: Holmes tells Watson that Miss Stapleton is Stapleton’s wife and that the case is murder. A scream sounds across the moor, and they find a body in Sir Henry’s clothes: it is Selden, wearing the baronet’s old wardrobe, run down by the hound. Stapleton arrives, masks his disappointment, and hears that Holmes is going home. At the Hall Holmes sees Stapleton’s face in the portrait of Hugo. Laura Lyons, shown proof that Stapleton is married, confesses that he dictated her letter.

scenes.title: Death on the Moor
scenes.summary: The sister who is a wife, a yell of horror, a ruddy tweed suit, and a beard.

scenes.title: Fixing the Nets
scenes.summary: The wicked Hugo’s portrait, a pretended departure, a photograph from York, and Lestrade on the London express.

structure.label: Chapter XIV
structure.title: The hound
structure.summary: Holmes, Watson and Lestrade lie in wait near Merripit House while Sir Henry dines there. Fog rolls in from the mire. As Sir Henry walks home the hound bursts out of the fog, glowing with fire, and Holmes shoots it dead at his throat. Upstairs they find Mrs Stapleton bound and beaten. Next morning she leads them to the path through the mire, where they find Sir Henry’s old boot; Stapleton is never seen again.

scenes.title: The ambush
scenes.summary: A creak at the out-house, a white fog like a sea, and a coal-black hound with flaming jaws.

scenes.title: The mire
scenes.summary: A woman tied to a beam, guiding wands, a boot marked Meyers, Toronto, and the bones of a spaniel.

structure.label: Chapter XV
structure.title: A retrospection
structure.summary: In Baker Street at the end of November, Holmes explains the case. Stapleton was the son of Rodger Baskerville, who had fled to South America; he had embezzled money in Costa Rica, run a school in Yorkshire as Vandeleur, and come to Devon to kill the two lives between him and the estate. He bought the hound in London, hid it on an island in the mire, and used his wife and Laura Lyons as tools. Holmes can only guess how Stapleton meant to claim his inheritance, and takes Watson to the opera.

scenes.title: A Retrospection
scenes.summary: Ross and Mangles of the Fulham Road, a scent of white jessamine, the servant Anthony, and a box for Les Huguenots.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.role: Consulting detective, who works the case in secret from a hut on the moor
characters.summary: Holmes treats the legend as a fairy tale and the footmark as material. He sends Watson to Devon, pretends to be busy with a blackmail case in London, and lives in a prehistoric hut, fed by the boy Cartwright, to watch without being watched. He is outwitted in London by a man who gives the cabman his name, and he admits that he nearly lost his client by waiting to make his case complete.
characters.clue: He lets his friend believe he is busy with a blackmailer in London while he lives in a stone hut, supplied by a boy from a messenger office.

characters.name: Dr John Watson
characters.role: Narrator, sent to Dartmoor to guard Sir Henry and report
characters.summary: Watson does most of the detective work in this book. He follows Barrymore at night, questions Laura Lyons, tracks the boy to the hut and waits there with his revolver. His letters are full of the moor’s atmosphere and of his own suspicions, some wrong, and he insists on common sense against the peasants’ fiend dog. He is hurt when he learns that Holmes has been on the moor all along, reading his reports.
characters.clue: He writes long letters from Devon to Baker Street, and throws down a cigarette marked Bradley, Oxford Street, at the door of an empty hut.

characters.name: Sir Henry Baskerville
characters.role: The heir, a young baronet raised in Canada and the United States
characters.summary: Small, sturdy, dark-eyed and about thirty, he has the fiery temper of the Baskervilles and the manners of the American West. He refuses to be frightened away from the home of his own people, plans electric lamps for the drive, and falls quickly in love with Miss Stapleton. He does as Holmes tells him and walks home across the moor, not knowing he is the bait, and survives the hound only to suffer a breakdown; he and Mortimer leave on a voyage round the world.
characters.clue: He buys new brown boots in the Strand, loses one of them, then loses an old black one, and says there is no devil in hell who will keep him from his home.

characters.name: Jack Stapleton
characters.role: A naturalist at Merripit House; in fact Rodger Baskerville, next in line after Sir Henry
characters.summary: Small, prim, flaxen-haired, with a butterfly-net and a tin box for specimens, he is a recognised authority on moths and one of the few people who know the paths through the Grimpen Mire. He is also the son of Sir Charles’s disgraced younger brother, an embezzler and a former schoolmaster under another name, who passes his wife off as his sister, murders Sir Charles with a painted hound and plans to kill Sir Henry the same way. He disappears into the mire in the fog.
characters.clue: He chases a moth called Cyclopides across a bog, and Holmes finds his face under the plumed hat of an old portrait.
characters.firstAppearance: Chapter VII (in person); Chapter IV (in disguise)

relationships.label: husband of, passing her off as his sister

characters.name: Beryl Stapleton
characters.role: Passed off as Stapleton’s sister; in fact his wife, born Beryl Garcia in Costa Rica
characters.summary: Tall, dark and elegant, with a curious lisp, she is darker than any brunette Watson has seen in England. Afraid of her husband, who beats her, she warns Watson, whom she takes for Sir Henry, to go back to London, and she composes the warning letter from words cut out of The Times. When she learns of the plot against Sir Henry and of her husband’s affair, she turns against him; he ties her up, and afterwards she leads Holmes to his path through the mire.
characters.clue: She sends a warning made of words cut from a newspaper and addressed in a disguised hand, and she planted the guiding wands through the mire.

characters.name: Dr James Mortimer
characters.role: Country doctor at Grimpen and executor of Sir Charles’s will
characters.summary: Tall, thin and absent-minded, a former house-surgeon at Charing Cross who gave up a London career to marry, he writes on atavism and covets Holmes’s skull. He brings the case to Baker Street, half believing in the hound, and withheld the footprints from the inquest because a man of science shrinks from seeming to endorse a superstition. He loses his curly-haired spaniel to the hound.
characters.clue: He leaves his stick behind in Baker Street, excavates a prehistoric barrow, and wrote a prize essay asking whether disease is a reversion.

characters.name: John Barrymore
characters.summary: Tall, handsome and pale, with a square black beard, he is the first suspect: he found Sir Charles’s body, benefits from the will, and walks the corridors at night. His secret turns out to be loyalty to his wife, who is feeding her brother, the escaped convict. In gratitude for Sir Henry’s silence he reveals the letter signed L. L., and Sir Henry’s old clothes, passed to Selden, cost the convict his life.
characters.clue: He holds a candle to an upper window facing the moor at two in the morning, and his family have served the Hall for four generations.

characters.name: Eliza Barrymore
characters.role: Housekeeper at the Hall, and the convict’s sister
characters.summary: A heavy, solid, intensely respectable woman whom Watson hears sobbing in the night. Her maiden name was Selden, and to her the Notting Hill murderer is still the curly-headed little brother she nursed. She takes the blame for the signals and weeps bitterly when he dies.
characters.clue: Her telltale eyes are red on the first morning, and she remembers a murderer as the little boy she played with.

characters.name: Selden
characters.role: The Notting Hill murderer, escaped from Princetown
characters.summary: A convict whose death sentence was commuted because of doubts about his sanity, he hides on the moor, fed by his sister and her husband. Watson sees his evil yellow face over a rock like one of the old savages of the burrows. Wearing Sir Henry’s cast-off clothes, he is hunted down by the hound and dies falling over a cliff.
characters.clue: An escaped murderer hiding on the moor, he answers a candle in a window with a candle of his own.

characters.name: Laura Lyons
characters.role: Frankland’s daughter, a typist in Coombe Tracey
characters.summary: Deserted by the artist she married against her father’s wishes, and helped into a typewriting business by Sir Charles, Stapleton and Mortimer, she hopes to divorce her husband and marry Stapleton. At his dictation she writes asking Sir Charles to meet her at the gate at ten, and he then stops her from going. Shown proof that he is married, she tells Holmes everything.
characters.clue: Her initials are found on the charred end of a letter, and she works at a Remington typewriter in Coombe Tracey.

characters.name: Mr Frankland
characters.role: A litigious old man of Lafter Hall
characters.summary: Red-faced, white-haired and choleric, he spends his fortune on lawsuits for the pleasure of fighting and is carried in triumph or burned in effigy by the villagers of Fernworthy. He has disowned his daughter. From his roof he sweeps the moor with a telescope, and his spite against the police leads Watson to the boy and the hut.
characters.clue: He has established a right of way across old Middleton’s park and watches the moor from his roof through a telescope on a tripod.

characters.name: Sir Charles Baskerville
characters.role: The late baronet, found dead in the yew alley
characters.summary: A widower who made a fortune in South Africa and came home to restore the Hall and help the countryside. He took the family legend so seriously that he would not cross the moor at night, and his heart was weak. Lured to the moor-gate by a letter, he saw the painted hound and ran down the alley until he fell dead.
characters.clue: The ash dropped twice from his cigar while he waited at a wicket-gate, and his footprints seemed to change to tiptoe.

characters.name: Hugo Baskerville
characters.role: The wicked ancestor of the legend
characters.summary: In the time of the Great Rebellion he abducted a yeoman’s daughter, vowed his body and soul to the Powers of Evil to catch her when she escaped, and was found on the moor with his throat torn out by a black beast shaped like a hound. His portrait in the dining-hall, dated 1647, shows a prim, hard, stern face.
characters.clue: He set the hounds on a girl who climbed down the ivy from his house, and his portrait, in black velvet and lace, hangs in the banqueting-hall.

characters.name: Lestrade
characters.summary: A small, wiry bulldog of a man who arrives on the London express with an unsigned warrant, and who now looks at Holmes with reverence. When the hound breaks out of the fog he yells with terror and throws himself on the ground.
characters.clue: He comes down by the London express with an unsigned warrant and keeps something in his hip-pocket.

themes.name: Superstition
themes.summary: A family legend is set against a detective who has hitherto confined his investigations to this world. Mortimer half believes in the hound; the peasants describe it with hell-fire; Sir Henry is shaken by its cry; Watson clings to his common sense. The legend is finally explained by a dog from a dealer in the Fulham Road and a paste of phosphorus, but the book gets much of its power from the fear it claims to dispel.
themes.development: The manuscript of 1742; a realm in which detectives are helpless; the devil’s agents of flesh and blood; the cry on the moor; common sense; phosphorus; the family ghost laid.

themes.name: Proof
themes.summary: Holmes knows early who the murderer is, and the problem is proving it. A death from fright leaves no mark; a hound that never bites cannot be linked to its master; no jury would believe the story. The case is built from small material facts, a boot, a cut newspaper, cigar ash, a smell of white jessamine, and finally from a trap in which Sir Henry is the bait.
themes.development: The stick; the Times leader; two boots; the cigar ash; a photograph from York; it is not what we know, but what we can prove.

themes.name: Inheritance and the family curse
themes.summary: Everything turns on who inherits: a baronetcy, an entailed estate and a fortune of nearly a million from South Africa. The legend makes inheritance a curse passed down the generations for Hugo’s sin, and the real danger is an heir, the disgraced younger brother’s son, who wants the estate. Sir Henry means to restore the grandeur of his line; Stapleton means to take it.
themes.development: The warning to his sons; seven hundred and forty thousand pounds; the entail; the Desmonds; the portrait; the three ways of claiming the property.

themes.name: Heredity and the throwback
themes.summary: Like many books of its time, this one is interested in what the body inherits. Mortimer writes on atavism and reversion and reads skulls; Selden’s face looks like a prehistoric savage’s; Holmes sees Stapleton in Hugo’s portrait and calls him a throw-back, physical and spiritual. Doyle takes these ideas half seriously and half as comedy, as in Mortimer’s wish for a cast of Holmes’s skull.
themes.development: Some Freaks of Atavism; the covetable skull; the Celt and the Ivernian; the evil yellow face; the throw-back in the portrait.

themes.name: The moor
themes.summary: Dartmoor is the book’s great presence: vast, barren, granite-flecked, scattered with the huts of prehistoric men and hiding the Grimpen Mire, where a false step means death. It carries Watson out of modern England, shelters a convict and a detective, and at the end swallows the murderer. The moor is where the legend becomes believable.
themes.development: The first sight of the moor; the mire and the pony; the stone huts; the man on the tor; the fog like a sea; for ever buried.

themes.name: Disguise and false identity
themes.summary: Almost no one is who they seem. Stapleton wears a false beard in London, gives the cabman Holmes’s name, has been Vandeleur, and is really a Baskerville; his wife passes as his sister; Holmes hides as a tourist in a hut; Selden dies in Sir Henry’s clothes. Holmes says the first quality of a criminal investigator is to see through a disguise.
themes.development: The black beard; You have been driving Mr. Sherlock Holmes; the sister who is a wife; the tourist in the tweed suit; the dead man in the ruddy tweed; the portrait.

themes.name: Women under a man’s control
themes.summary: The two women closest to the crime are both Stapleton’s instruments. His wife passes as his sister under threats and blows, and Laura Lyons writes the fatal letter because he has promised to marry her. Each knows or suspects part of the truth and is silenced by fear or hope. Mrs Barrymore, loyal to a murderous brother, completes a picture of women bound to dangerous men.
themes.development: The warning on the path; the curious lisp; the letter signed L. L.; Prove it to me!; the weal across her neck; mind and soul tortured.

techniques.name: The chain of inference
techniques.definition: Reasoning from small observed details to confident conclusions.
techniques.inThisBook: Holmes opens the book by reading a walking-stick and correcting Watson’s reading of it, and continues with the Times leader, the hotel ink and the boots. Doyle then keeps Holmes off the stage for half the book, so that the reader must reason with Watson from partial evidence.

techniques.name: Watson’s narration
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.inThisBook: Watson writes after the event, and he admits that some suspicions recorded in his letters proved unfounded. His admiration for Holmes, his sensitivity to the moor and his occasional wounded pride shape what the reader feels.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: A story told partly through letters or documents written by the characters.
techniques.inThisBook: For three chapters the narrative becomes Watson’s reports to Holmes and extracts from his diary. The switch gives immediacy and uncertainty, since the letters were written without knowing the outcome, and it prepares the surprise that Holmes has been reading them in a hut a few miles away.

techniques.name: The Gothic explained
techniques.definition: The stock furniture of Gothic writing put to a particular use.
techniques.inThisBook: A cursed family, an ancestral portrait, a gloomy hall with a minstrel’s gallery, a woman sobbing in the night, candles at windows, a spectral hound: Doyle uses the whole Gothic inheritance, and then gives each item a natural cause.

techniques.name: Misdirection
techniques.definition: Leading the reader towards a false suspect or explanation.
techniques.inThisBook: Suspicion falls in turn on the black-bearded Barrymore, the sobbing housekeeper, the mysterious man on the tor and Frankland’s telescope; each is explained, and the friendly naturalist who explains the moor is the murderer.

techniques.name: The material clue
techniques.definition: A physical object on which the solution turns.
techniques.inThisBook: The boots are the key clue: a new one stolen and returned, an old one stolen in its place, which tells Holmes that the enemy needs a scent for a real dog. The cut-out Times leader, the cigar ash and a cigarette stub marked Bradley do similar work.

techniques.name: Landscape and weather
techniques.definition: Place and weather made to press on the people living in them.
techniques.inThisBook: Doyle times the weather to the story: sunlight and red earth at the arrival, rain and fog in Watson’s diary, moonlight for the man on the tor, and a creeping white fog that nearly wrecks Holmes’s plan at the climax.

techniques.name: The legend as prophecy
techniques.definition: A statement about the future that shapes the action by being believed.
techniques.inThisBook: The manuscript warns the family to avoid the moor in the dark hours when the powers of evil are exalted, and Holmes and Sir Henry both repeat the phrase. The legend works as a prophecy because the murderer makes it come true.

quotations.text: you are a conductor of light. Some people without possessing genius have a remarkable power of stimulating it.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Watson has just read Dr Mortimer’s stick, and Holmes praises him.
quotations.analysis: Holmes’s compliment is backhanded, and it defines the partnership: Watson has no genius, but he stimulates it. His wrong guesses guide Holmes towards the truth, as Holmes explains a moment later. The phrase also describes Watson’s role in this book, carrying a light he does not generate himself.

quotations.text: It is not my intention to be fulsome, but I confess that I covet your skull.
quotations.speaker: Dr James Mortimer
quotations.context: Mortimer has just met Holmes and admired his dolichocephalic head.
quotations.analysis: Mortimer’s enthusiasm for skulls is comic, and it belongs to the science of his day, which tried to read character and race in the shape of the head. The theme of inherited type will return seriously in the throw-back, but here Doyle lets Holmes answer with a cigarette.

quotations.text: standing over Hugo, and plucking at his throat, there stood a foul thing, a great, black beast, shaped like a hound, yet larger than any hound that ever mortal eye has rested upon.
quotations.context: The manuscript of 1742 describes what the revellers found on the moor.
quotations.analysis: In the language of an old family paper, all long piling clauses and archaic ceremony, the legend gives the book its monster. Shaped like a hound, yet larger than any hound is the phrase the whole book tests. Watson’s description of the real hound in chapter XIV echoes it.

quotations.text: that which is clearly known hath less terror than that which is but hinted at and guessed.
quotations.context: The writer of the manuscript explains why he has set the story down for his sons.
quotations.analysis: Here the ancestor states the principle of every good mystery, and the book follows it. The hound is heard, rumoured and glimpsed long before it is seen, and when it is finally clearly known, dead and daubed with phosphorus, its terror is gone.

quotations.text: Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!
quotations.speaker: Dr James Mortimer
quotations.context: Mortimer’s voice sinks almost to a whisper as he tells what he saw near Sir Charles’s body.
quotations.analysis: This line ended the first part in The Strand in August 1901, and readers had to wait a month to learn more. Footprints are material evidence, the kind Holmes trusts, and yet they point to the legend, so the clue sets the rational and the supernatural against each other from the start.

quotations.text: There is a realm in which the most acute and most experienced of detectives is helpless.
quotations.speaker: Dr James Mortimer
quotations.context: Holmes has asked why Mortimer did not call him in immediately.
quotations.analysis: A man of science admits that he half believes in the supernatural, and he challenges the detective’s method directly. The novel is built as the answer to this sentence. Mortimer is honest, learned and wrong, and his doubt gives the reader permission to be frightened.

quotations.text: I have hitherto confined my investigations to this world ... In a modest way I have combated evil, but to take on the Father of Evil himself would, perhaps, be too ambitious a task.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes replies to Mortimer’s suggestion that the thing is supernatural.
quotations.analysis: Holmes answers the supernatural with irony, and the joke is also a statement of method. He will not argue about the devil; he insists that the footmark is material. The phrase the Father of Evil keeps the legend’s language alive even as he declines it.

quotations.text: The world is full of obvious things which nobody by any chance ever observes.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes has worked out that Watson spent the whole day at his club.
quotations.analysis: The maxim sums up the Holmes method and flatters the reader into trying it. The case will turn on obvious things nobody observes: which boot was stolen, which side of the path the prints were on, which way a frightened man ran.

quotations.text: He was running, Watson—running desperately, running for his life
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes corrects the inquest’s idea that Sir Charles walked on tiptoe.
quotations.analysis: A single deduction changes the meaning of the evidence: the footprints that seemed to show a man on tiptoe show a man running until he burst his heart. The repeated word running builds the horror of the scene out of a detail, and it raises the question the rest of the book must answer: running from what?

quotations.text: As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.
quotations.context: The warning sent to Sir Henry at the Northumberland Hotel, made of printed words pasted on paper, with only the word moor printed by hand in ink.
quotations.analysis: Holmes treats the warning as a puzzle and a clue about its sender: he traces the words to a Times leader and reasons that an educated person disguised the hand. Only late in the book do we learn that Beryl Stapleton sent it, the one act she dared against her husband.

quotations.text: Say, rather, into the region where we balance probabilities and choose the most likely. It is the scientific use of the imagination
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Mortimer has accused Holmes of guesswork about the hotel ink.
quotations.analysis: Holmes describes detection as the balancing of probabilities, and calls it the scientific use of the imagination, always with some material basis to start from. The phrase answers the charge that he merely guesses, and it describes what Doyle asks of the reader: to imagine freely and stay tied to the evidence.

quotations.text: There is no devil in hell, Mr. Holmes, and there is no man upon earth who can prevent me from going to the home of my own people
quotations.speaker: Sir Henry Baskerville
quotations.context: Holmes has asked whether it is safe for Sir Henry to go to Baskerville Hall.
quotations.analysis: Sir Henry’s answer shows the fiery temper of the Baskervilles, which Watson notices immediately. His courage is real and so is his pride in family, the feeling the murderer counts on. The devil and the man are the two possible enemies weighed throughout the story.

quotations.text: A false step yonder means death to man or beast.
quotations.speaker: Jack Stapleton
quotations.context: Stapleton shows Watson the bright green spots of the Grimpen Mire.
quotations.analysis: Stapleton, the friendly naturalist, introduces the landscape’s great danger, and his own boast that he alone knows the paths. The irony is complete by the end: the mire hides his hound and, somewhere in the fog, swallows the man himself.

quotations.text: It is so vast, and so barren, and so mysterious.
quotations.speaker: Jack Stapleton
quotations.context: Walking Watson to Merripit House, Stapleton looks round over the undulating downs.
quotations.analysis: Stapleton speaks of the moor like a lover, and his delight seems real: he knows its secrets better than anyone. One of those secrets, the reader learns, is his hound, kept on an island in the mire, which gives the line a second meaning on rereading.

quotations.text: Go straight back to London, instantly.
quotations.speaker: Beryl Stapleton
quotations.context: On the moor path, the woman Watson takes for Miss Stapleton mistakes him for Sir Henry.
quotations.analysis: Beryl’s warning comes before any introduction and is the book’s clearest early hint that something is wrong at Merripit House. Beryl risks her husband’s anger to say it, then covers it with talk of orchids. Her mistaken identity is the first of many.

quotations.text: Life has become like that great Grimpen Mire, with little green patches everywhere into which one may sink and with no guide to point the track.
quotations.speaker: Dr John Watson
quotations.context: Watson begs Miss Stapleton to explain her warning.
quotations.analysis: Watson makes the landscape a figure for the mystery itself, and the image fits the plot’s method: every apparently solid fact may give way. The line also shows how quickly the moor has entered his imagination.

quotations.text: When you are once out upon its bosom you have left all traces of modern England behind you
quotations.context: Watson’s first report to Holmes from Baskerville Hall opens with the moor.
quotations.analysis: Watson’s letters begin with atmosphere before facts, and he apologises for it. On the moor he feels its vastness and its grim charm, and he steps out of his own century among the huts and graves of forgotten people. That is the setting in which a legend can seem believable to a sensible man.

quotations.text: you would feel that his presence there was more natural than your own.
quotations.context: Watson imagines a skin-clad prehistoric man crawling out of one of the stone huts.
quotations.analysis: On the moor the modern visitor feels like the intruder. The idea of the prehistoric past lingering in the present links the landscape with the book’s interest in heredity and the throw-back, and it prepares the convict’s face, like an old savage’s, over the rocks.

quotations.text: My unhappy brother is starving on the moor. We cannot let him perish at our very gates.
quotations.speaker: Eliza Barrymore
quotations.context: Mrs Barrymore explains the candle her husband holds to the window at night.
quotations.analysis: Barrymore’s secret, which made him the chief suspect, is an act of family loyalty. The revelation clears one mystery and adds a second fugitive to the moor. Mrs Barrymore’s love for a murderer is one of the book’s few purely human moments.

quotations.text: He might have been the very spirit of that terrible place.
quotations.context: After the chase of the convict, Watson sees a tall figure standing on a tor against the moon.
quotations.analysis: Watson describes the mysterious watcher as a ghost, and the reader is invited to wonder whether he is enemy or supernatural. The figure is Holmes, and the moment is typical of the book: a Gothic image that turns out to have the most rational explanation of all.

quotations.text: if I have one quality upon earth it is common sense, and nothing will persuade me to believe in such a thing.
quotations.context: In his diary Watson reviews the case on a foggy day.
quotations.analysis: Watson insists on common sense in the very entry where he admits he has twice heard the hound. The protest shows how far the moor has shaken him. Doyle gives the reader the same double position: sceptical in principle and frightened in practice.

quotations.text: Please, please, as you are a gentleman, burn this letter, and be at the gate by ten o'clock.
quotations.speaker: Laura Lyons
quotations.context: The postscript that survived in the grate of Sir Charles’s study, as Barrymore reports it.
quotations.analysis: A charred scrap of paper is the missing link between Sir Charles and the gate. Its pleading tone, and its request to burn it, suggest scandal before crime. It was dictated by Stapleton, who used a woman’s trouble to draw his victim out at night.

quotations.text: It is a lovely evening, my dear Watson ... I really think that you will be more comfortable outside than in.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Watson waits with a cocked revolver in the stone hut for its tenant to return.
quotations.analysis: Suspense collapses into Holmes’s ironic courtesy. The unseen watcher of the moor is the detective, and the Gothic stranger turns out to be the most familiar voice in the book. Watson’s relief is mixed with hurt at having been deceived.

quotations.text: It is not what we know, but what we can prove.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: After Selden’s death Watson wants to seize Stapleton immediately.
quotations.analysis: Holmes states the book’s central difficulty in one line. He knows the murderer and his method, yet a death from fright leaves no case a jury would accept, so the plot must now produce proof, at the risk of Sir Henry’s life.

quotations.text: Evil indeed is the man who has not one woman to mourn him.
quotations.context: Mrs Barrymore weeps bitterly for her brother Selden.
quotations.analysis: Watson’s moral is sentimental and generous. To the world Selden was half animal and half demon; to his sister he was a child who clung to her hand. The line softens the book’s treatment of its most brutal figure, and contrasts with the cold villain who will have no one to mourn him.

quotations.text: The face of Stapleton had sprung out of the canvas.
quotations.context: Holmes holds a candle to the portrait of Hugo Baskerville and covers the hat and ringlets with his arm.
quotations.analysis: With the portrait, the legend becomes evidence. By hiding the costume Holmes shows the face beneath, and the family resemblance supplies the motive the case lacked: Stapleton is a Baskerville with designs on the succession.

quotations.text: A study of family portraits is enough to convert a man to the doctrine of reincarnation. The fellow is a Baskerville—that is evident.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes explains the resemblance between Stapleton and the wicked Hugo.
quotations.analysis: Holmes jokes that family portraits could convert a man to reincarnation, then states the fact that matters: Stapleton is a Baskerville. A moment before, he has called the likeness a throw-back, physical and spiritual, borrowing the vocabulary of heredity, so that the curse of the Baskervilles becomes a bad strain returning in a descendant.

quotations.text: I knew him ... But if he had kept faith with me I should always have done so with him.
quotations.speaker: Laura Lyons
quotations.context: Holmes has asked whether she had suspicions of Stapleton.
quotations.analysis: Laura Lyons admits she suspected him and stayed silent out of love. Her loyalty broke only when she learned he was married. Holmes tells her she has had a fortunate escape, having walked for months near the edge of a precipice.

quotations.text: A hound it was, an enormous coal-black hound, but not such a hound as mortal eyes have ever seen.
quotations.context: The creature bursts out of the fog on the track behind Sir Henry.
quotations.analysis: The long-awaited monster appears in a sentence that echoes the legend’s larger than any hound that ever mortal eye has rested upon. For a moment Watson’s description is as Gothic as the manuscript, with fire bursting from the jaws, before the narrative restores a real, wounded animal.

quotations.text: We've laid the family ghost once and for ever.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Sir Henry, reviving, asks what it was that attacked him.
quotations.analysis: The hound is dead, painted with phosphorus, and Holmes lays the ghost with a dry phrase. The supernatural has been explained, and yet the book’s next pages return to the mire, the fog and a man vanishing, so the relief is not complete.

quotations.text: It is my mind and soul that he has tortured and defiled.
quotations.speaker: Beryl Stapleton
quotations.context: Released from the beam where her husband tied her, she shows her bruised arms.
quotations.analysis: Beryl names a cruelty the detective plot has no category for. The bruises are evidence; the torture of mind and soul is not. Her outburst is the strongest statement in the book of what Stapleton did to the women he used.

quotations.text: this cold and cruel-hearted man is for ever buried.
quotations.context: Beyond the boot in the mire the searchers find no footprints; somewhere in the heart of the great Grimpen Mire, Watson writes, the morass has sucked Stapleton in.
quotations.analysis: The villain gets no trial and no confession. The moor takes him, as it took the ponies, and the ending leaves him unseen, which is a Gothic and not a legal conclusion. Watson’s solemn language makes the mire an instrument of justice.

quotations.text: The past and the present are within the field of my inquiry, but what a man may do in the future is a hard question to answer.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Watson asks how Stapleton could have claimed the estate without arousing suspicion.
quotations.analysis: Holmes admits a limit to his method, and the book ends with an unsolved question alongside the solved crime. Detection reconstructs what has happened; it cannot fully predict a person. The admission gives the final chapter a modesty the legend never had.

timeline.label: A Study in Scarlet
timeline.detail: Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson first appear, in Beeton’s Christmas Annual.

timeline.label: The Final Problem
timeline.detail: In The Strand Magazine for December, Doyle sends Holmes over the Reichenbach Falls with Professor Moriarty.

timeline.label: The Hound in The Strand
timeline.detail: The first of nine monthly parts appears in August, with a footnote crediting Fletcher Robinson with the story’s inception.

timeline.label: The first edition
timeline.detail: George Newnes publishes the novel on 25 March, dedicated to Robinson; the American edition follows on 15 April.

timeline.label: The Empty House
timeline.detail: Holmes returns in a new story, explaining that he never fell at Reichenbach at all.

timeline.label: Conan Doyle dies
timeline.detail: On 7 July, at his home in Sussex.

timeline.label: Basil Rathbone’s Hound
timeline.detail: Twentieth Century-Fox films the novel with Basil Rathbone as Holmes and Nigel Bruce as Watson.

timeline.label: Hammer’s Hound
timeline.detail: Hammer Films makes the first colour film of the story, with Peter Cushing as Holmes.

places.name: Baker Street, London
places.note: Where Mortimer brings the case, and where Holmes explains it at the end of November.

places.name: Paddington Station
places.note: Where Watson, Sir Henry and Mortimer take the ten-thirty train for Devon.

places.name: Princetown, Dartmoor
places.note: The great convict prison from which Selden escapes, fourteen miles from the Hall on Holmes’s map.

places.name: Dartmoor
places.note: The granite moor, with its tors, stone huts and bogs, on which Doyle placed the invented Baskerville Hall, Grimpen and the Grimpen Mire.

places.name: Hindhead, Surrey
places.note: Where Doyle lived and signed the dedication to Robinson.

criticalViews.summary: The classic reading sees the novel as a contest between a family legend and the rational detective, which reason wins: the hound comes from a dealer’s shop, its fire is phosphorus, and every Gothic mystery has a material cause. On this view the book reassures its readers that the modern world is knowable.
criticalViews.counter: The book draws its power from the fear it claims to dispel. Holmes is absent for half the story, the moor and its prehistoric ruins remain strange, and the murderer vanishes without trace into the mire. Many readers remember the hound more than the explanation.

criticalViews.summary: Some critics read the book in the light of late-Victorian anxieties about heredity and degeneration. Mortimer measures skulls and writes on atavism, Selden looks like a prehistoric savage, and Holmes calls Stapleton a throw-back to Hugo, physical and spiritual. The villain’s wickedness seems to be inherited, like the family face.
criticalViews.counter: Doyle treats the pseudo-science with irony as well as interest. Mortimer’s craniology is comic, the case is solved by evidence, and the throw-back is a detective’s phrase in a moment of excitement, while the real motive is money.

criticalViews.summary: Feminist readers point out that the women know the most and say the least. Beryl Stapleton is beaten into passing as a sister and silenced by fear; Laura Lyons is controlled by a promise of marriage; Mrs Barrymore is bound by loyalty to a brother. The detective plot depends on their eventual testimony.
criticalViews.counter: The book gives these women little inner life, and Holmes’s final explanation reduces Beryl’s rebellion to a remark about Spanish blood. The novel notices coercion without making it its subject.

essayQuestions.question: How does Conan Doyle create and then explain the supernatural in The Hound of the Baskervilles?
plan: Begin with the manuscript of 1742 and Mortimer’s ‘realm in which the most acute and most experienced of detectives is helpless’.
Analyse how the hound is heard and glimpsed before it is seen: the moan on the moor, the footprints, the peasants’ stories.
Examine Watson’s letters and diary, and his insistence on common sense.
Discuss the climax: the hound in the fog, phosphorus and the family ghost laid.
Consider whether the explanation fully dispels the fear the book creates.

essayQuestions.question: How is the moor presented, and why does it matter to the novel?
plan: Start with Watson’s first sight of the moor and the arrival at the Hall.
Look at the Grimpen Mire and Stapleton’s knowledge of its paths.
Consider the stone huts and the sense of the prehistoric past.
Analyse the weather: fog, rain, moonlight and the creeping fog at the climax.
Conclude on the mire as the place that swallows the murderer.

essayQuestions.question: What is the importance of Watson in The Hound of the Baskervilles?
plan: Examine the opening with the stick: Watson as a conductor of light.
Show how Holmes’s absence makes Watson the investigator in Devon.
Analyse the letters and diary as a narrative method.
Discuss the revelation at the hut and Watson’s feelings about it.
Evaluate what the book gains from seeing Holmes through Watson’s eyes.

discussionQuestions: Why does Conan Doyle keep Holmes away from Dartmoor for so much of the novel?
What does the portrait of Hugo add to the case?
Is Holmes right to use Sir Henry as bait?
How far does the novel take the idea of inherited wickedness seriously?
What do Beryl Stapleton and Laura Lyons each know, and why do they stay silent?
Why might the novel end with Stapleton lost in the mire, and not on trial?

related.why: The second Holmes novel, where Watson falls in love and the solution lies in an old crime committed abroad.
The first collection of Holmes stories from The Strand, where the reader first learns the method Holmes uses on Mortimer’s stick.
An earlier English detective novel told through several narrators’ documents, with an Indian curse and a country house.
Another novel in which moorland and an inherited estate shape violent passions across generations.
A Gothic novel of the same decade told through letters and journals, with a stranger who arrives to claim a place in England.
